 A Bigger Social Security Raise Is Coming in 2027 - Here’s What to Do Now
 Josh Koebert 2026년 11월 5일 목 오전 10:39 UTC 0 Social
 Security beneficiaries got welcome news this month. Their monthly checks are
 going up by more in 2027 than they did this year. For millions of retirees
 counting on that payment to help pay for rent , groceries, and medical bills, any
 increase feels like good news. But a bigger raise on paper doesn't always
 translate into a bigger cushion in your bank account.
 Before the new amount shows up in January, it's worth taking a clear-eyed look
 at what's actually changing, what isn't, and what you can do in the meantime to
 make sure the extra money works as hard as possible for you.
 Find Out: 13 moves seniors could benefit from but often forget about. 
 How the 2027 COLA compares with 2026
 The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment
 (COLA) for 2027, according to the agency's October 2026 announcement. That's
 noticeably larger than the 2.8% COLA that took effect in January 2026. 
 The COLA
 is a yearly adjustment tied to inflation, specifically changes in the Consumer
 Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), as measured by
 the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
 In dollar terms, the SSA estimates the average retired worker's benefit will
 rise from $2,095 a month in 2026 to $2,170 a month after the 2027 COLA takes
 effect, an increase of about $75 a month on average, per the SSA's 2027 COLA
 fact sheet. The adjustment applies to Social Security retirement benefits
 starting in January 2027, while increased Supplemental Security Income (SSI)
 payments begin December 31, 2026.
 It's a bigger bump than last year's, but it's also a reminder that COLAs are
 designed to help benefits keep pace with rising prices, not to deliver a true
 increase in purchasing power. If your costs rose faster than 3.6% this year, in
 areas like health care or housing, the raise may simply help you tread water
 rather than get ahead.

 Review your essential expenses now, not in January
 Rather than waiting to see the new benefit amount and reacting afterward,
 consider using the next couple of months to take stock of your fixed costs:
 housing, utilities, insurance premiums, prescriptions, and groceries. Compare
 what you're spending now with what you were spending a year ago. If certain
 costs have climbed more than 3.6%, the COLA alone may not fully offset them.
 This kind of review can help you spot where a budget shortfall might reemerge
 even after the raise lands, so you're not caught off guard in the spring.
 Check your personalized COLA notice carefully
 The SSA sends every beneficiary a personalized notice showing the exact new
 benefit amount and any deductions, such as Medicare premiums, according to the
 agency's 2027 COLA announcement. 
 For 2027, beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare
 can expect to see their updated premium information in their my Social Security
 online account's Message Center starting in late November 2026. Those without an
 online account will receive the notice by mail in December.
 Creating or logging into a my Social Security account can let you view this
 notice up to about three weeks earlier than a mailed letter, provided you've
 opted into digital notices by November 18, 2026, according to SSA's advocate
 communications.

 Factor in Medicare costs before celebrating the raise
 For many retirees, Medicare Part B premiums are deducted directly from Social
 Security checks, which means a chunk of any COLA can disappear before it ever
 reaches your account. 
 The standard Medicare Part B premium for 2026 is $202.90 a
 month, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).
 Higher-income beneficiaries pay more under the Income-Related Monthly Adjustment
 Amount (IRMAA). For example, individuals with 2024 income above $109,000 (or
 $218,000 for joint filers) pay a higher premium tier, up to $689.90 a month at
 the highest income levels, according to CMS's 2026 premium tables.
 CMS has not yet finalized the 2027 standard Part B premium as of this writing;
 that figure, along with 2027 IRMAA brackets, will be available at Medicare.gov.
 Since Medicare premium increases can quietly eat into a COLA, it's worth
 checking your projected 2027 premium once it's published rather than assuming
 the full raise will land in your pocket.
 Consider whether additional income makes sense for your situation
 Some retirees look at a modest raise and wonder whether picking up part-time
 work could help close any remaining gap. That's a decision worth weighing with
 your full financial picture in mind, but it helps to understand the rules before
 deciding.
 If you're receiving retirement benefits before reaching full retirement age
 (FRA) and continue to work, the SSA applies an earnings test. For 2027, if
 you're under FRA for the entire year, you can earn up to $25,560 without any
 reduction in benefits; above that, the SSA withholds $1 in benefits for every $2
 earned over the limit, according to the SSA's 2027 fact sheet. 
 In the calendar
 year you reach FRA, a higher limit applies to earnings in the months before you
 turn FRA: $67,920 for 2027, with $1 withheld for every $3 earned above that
 amount. Once you reach full retirement age, which is 67 for anyone born in 1960
 or later, there's no limit on how much you can earn without affecting your
 benefit.
 Importantly, withheld benefits aren't gone forever. The SSA recalculates your
 benefit upward once you reach full retirement age to credit you for months when
 payments were reduced or withheld. Still, if you're weighing part-time work
 against your benefit amount, understanding these thresholds ahead of time can
 help you avoid an unwelcome surprise.
 Don't count on the raise to solve an existing shortfall
 If your budget has already been tight, it's tempting to view a bigger COLA as
 the fix. But a 3.6% increase on an average benefit of roughly $2,071 a month
 works out to about $75 more a month, not a windfall. For beneficiaries facing
 rising housing or health care costs, that amount may only partially offset
 what's already changed in their budget.
 Preparing now, rather than waiting for January's number, means looking honestly
 at whether your current spending plan is sustainable with or without the raise.
 The COLA is meant to help preserve the purchasing power you already have, not
 create new financial flexibility beyond that.

 Bottom line
 A 3.6% COLA for 2027 is a larger adjustment than the 2.8% increase retirees saw
 in 2026, and the SSA projects the average retired worker's benefit will climb
 from $2,095 to $2,170 a month. But the real impact on your budget depends on
 your personal expenses, your Medicare premiums, and whether you're still working
 and subject to the earnings test.
 Taking a few steps now, reviewing your
 expenses, reading your COLA notice carefully, and checking your projected
 Medicare costs, can help you understand exactly what the raise means for your
 situation before it arrives. For a personalized estimate of your future benefits, the SSA's online retirement estimator and your my Social Security
 account remain reliable tools for seeing where you stand financially .
